Soil cadmium in the planted plots fell to 3.1 mg per kilogram, a reduction of 63 % against the initial value.
Soil cadmium in the control plots ended at 7.9 mg per kilogram, a reduction of 6 % against the same initial value.
definitions: vetiver grass = Vetiveria zizanioides, a perennial grass planted for metal uptake from soil
surface layer = the upper soil layer from which samples were taken
dry mass = the mass of a sample after drying to constant mass

prose:
Cadmium uptake by vetiver grass (Vetiveria zizanioides, a perennial grass planted for metal uptake from soil) was measured in a replicated field trial on land beside a closed smelter. Initial soil cadmium was 8.4 mg per kilogram across the trial area. The trial held 4 planted plots and 4 unplanted control plots on the same soil unit, and every plot received the same rainfall and the same absence of irrigation across a full growing season. Planting density and cutting height were held constant across the planted plots, and the grass received no fertiliser during the season. Soil samples were composited from the surface layer (the upper soil layer from which samples were taken), dried, digested in acid, and measured by atomic absorption spectrometry. Harvested shoots were weighed fresh, dried to constant mass, and measured by the same instrument route as the soil samples.

Harvested shoot biomass reached 6.8 tonnes per hectare in the planted plots. Shoot cadmium concentration in the harvested biomass was 412 mg per kilogram of dry mass. The harvested shoots carried the removed cadmium off the plots in the harvested material, and the uptake route is consistent with the mass of cadmium missing from the planted soil at the end of the trial. Regrowth after cutting drew on the same root system, and the uptake measurement covers the harvested growth only.

Soil cadmium in the planted plots fell to 3.1 mg per kilogram at the end of the trial (a reduction of 63 % against the initial value). Soil cadmium in the control plots ended at 7.9 mg per kilogram (a reduction of 6 % against the same initial value). The contrast between the planted plots and the control plots assigns the larger fall to plant uptake. Leaching and sampling drift act on both sets of plots, and the control plots bound the size of both effects on the same soil unit. The result holds for the surface layer sampled in the trial, on the soil and drainage conditions of the trial area, and the deeper soil profile carries no measurement in the trial.

definitions: polymer electrolyte fuel cell = a fuel cell in which a polymer membrane carries protons between the electrodes
open-circuit voltage = the cell voltage at zero current
current density = current divided by the active electrode area, in amperes per square centimetre
activation loss = the voltage loss from the electrode reaction kinetics
ohmic loss = the voltage loss from ionic and electronic resistance in the cell
concentration loss = the voltage loss from reactant depletion at the electrode surface at high current
limits: The loss separation holds at the stated temperature and humidification; drier feed gas lies outside the tested conditions.
prose:
Voltage losses in a polymer electrolyte fuel cell (a fuel cell in which a polymer membrane carries protons between the electrodes) were measured on a single cell at 353 K with humidified hydrogen and air. Open-circuit voltage (the cell voltage at zero current) was 0.94 V. The membrane was a perfluorosulfonic acid membrane, and both electrodes carried platinum catalyst on carbon. Feed gases entered at ambient pressure, and the cell was held at temperature until the open-circuit voltage was stable before any load was applied. Polarisation data were recorded across the load range of the cell, and each loss term was separated by a named route: activation loss from the low-current slope, ohmic loss from the high-frequency resistance measured by impedance, and concentration loss from the departure of the high-current data from the ohmic line. The separation routes share the same polarisation curve, and the loss terms are reported at a single stated load.

At a current density of 1.2 amperes per square centimetre, activation loss (the voltage loss from the electrode reaction kinetics) was 0.19 V, ohmic loss (the voltage loss from ionic and electronic resistance in the cell) was 0.05 V, and concentration loss (the voltage loss from reactant depletion at the electrode surface at high current) was 0.02 V. The three losses sum to 0.26 V, and the operating voltage at that current density was 0.68 V. Activation loss is the largest term at the stated load, and the margin between the operating voltage and the open-circuit voltage is carried mainly by electrode kinetics rather than by membrane resistance. Concentration loss grows steeply as current density approaches the limiting current of the cathode, and the stated load sits below that region. Ohmic loss grew linearly with current across the measured range, and the growth matches a constant membrane resistance at fixed humidification. Repeat polarisation curves on the same cell reproduced the loss separation within the scatter of the impedance measurement. Hydrogen utilisation in the test was 85 %, and the loss separation holds at the stated temperature and humidification, with drier feed gas outside the tested conditions.

prose:
Stage efficiency in the liquid-liquid extraction of acetic acid from water into ethyl acetate was measured in a laboratory column. The feed carried 12.4 g of solute (the extracted component, acetic acid in this system) per litre. The column held 6 theoretical stages at the test condition, and the solvent-to-feed ratio was 1.5 by volume. Samples were taken from the raffinate (the diluent stream leaving the column after extraction) outlet and from stage sampling ports after the column reached steady state, and solute concentrations were measured by titration against a standard alkali. Steady state was judged on constant outlet concentrations across successive samples, and the stage profile was built from the port samples nearest the two ends of the column and the middle port. Each concentration was measured in duplicate, and duplicate agreement set the reporting precision of the profile.

Raffinate solute concentration was 1.9 g per litre, and solute extraction was 84.7 % of the feed solute. Murphree stage efficiency (the change in composition across a stage divided by the change that equilibrium with the leaving streams would give) averaged 78 % across the column, with stage values from 71 % to 84 %. Efficiency predicted from equilibrium stage calculations was 92 %. Stage efficiency was lowest near the feed inlet, where the driving force is largest and entrainment has the shortest path to the raffinate outlet. Stage efficiency near the solvent inlet stood closer to the column average, and the profile shape matches a column limited by phase separation at the feed end rather than by drop size along the whole height. The gap between the measured efficiency and the equilibrium prediction sits in the contacting rather than in the equilibrium data: entrainment of the dispersed phase and backmixing of the continuous phase both carry solute against the concentration gradient, and both grow with the agitation rate used in the test. The efficiency values hold at the stated solvent-to-feed ratio and feed concentration, and a leaner feed or a lower ratio lies outside the tested condition.

prose:
Fermentation kinetics of a lager yeast (Saccharomyces pastorianus, a bottom-fermenting yeast used in lager production) were measured in a laboratory fermenter on a malt wort (the sugar solution extracted from malted grain before fermentation). Initial sugar concentration was 118 g per litre. The fermenter was pitched with yeast from a propagated culture, aerated once at pitching, and then sealed against air ingress for the rest of the run. Wort composition was fixed across the run, and the pitching rate was set from the propagated culture count rather than from culture mass. Sugar and ethanol were measured on withdrawn samples by liquid chromatography, and yeast count was measured by haemocytometer under a microscope. Samples were drawn on a fixed schedule through the run, with denser sampling across the growth phase and sparser sampling as the sugar ran down.

Maximum specific growth rate (the rate of increase of cell count per unit cell count) was 0.31 per hour. Peak yeast count was 240 million cells per millilitre, reached as the sugar fell through the middle of its range. Growth slowed as ethanol accumulated, and the count declined after the peak as cells flocculated and settled to the base of the fermenter. The growth pattern matches a culture limited first by nitrogen and then by the ethanol the culture itself produced.

Final sugar concentration was 9 g per litre, and sugar consumption was 92.4 %. Final ethanol concentration was 5.6 % by volume. Fermentation temperature was held at 18 degrees Celsius, and the fermentation time was 96 hours. Attenuation was tracked on the same samples as the sugar measurement, and the two records agree on the end point of the fermentation. The residual sugar was mainly unfermentable dextrin rather than fermentable sugar, and the ethanol yield sits below the stoichiometric ceiling for the sugar consumed because carbon also left the wort as yeast biomass and as carbon dioxide through the airlock. The kinetics hold for the stated wort composition and pitching condition, and a wort of different nitrogen content lies outside the tested condition.

prose:
The goal of this worked example is a steady-state material balance around a reactor with recycle (the stream returned from the separator to the mixing point), and the outcome is a closed balance in which every stream flow is stated and the reactor balance is checked. You need no more than the balance itself: material in equals material out at steady state, applied first to the whole loop and then to the reactor. Work through the streams in the order the material moves.

Fresh feed enters at 100 kg per hour. Recycle returns 60 kg per hour to the mixing point (the junction where fresh feed and recycle meet), and the purge (a stream withdrawn from the loop so that inerts and unreacted material do not accumulate) removes 60 kg per hour from the separator outlet. Combined feed to the reactor is 160 kg per hour. Per-pass conversion (the fraction of the reactor feed converted in a single pass) in the reactor is 25 %. Converted material leaving as product is 40 kg per hour, and unreacted material leaving the reactor is 120 kg per hour. The separator sends the unreacted material back toward the mixing point, and the purge withdraws the share of that stream fixed by the purge setting.

The check closes the reactor balance: 40 kg per hour converted plus 120 kg per hour unreacted returns the 160 kg per hour combined feed. The balance shows the working of the loop in one place. Overall conversion stands above per-pass conversion because unreacted material passes through the reactor again rather than leaving with the product. The purge carries the cost of the arrangement: material withdrawn in the purge is material the reactor never sees again, and a purge set to zero lets inerts build up in the loop until the balance has no steady state at all. Set the purge from the inert content of the fresh feed, not from the product rate. The balance is a steady-state balance and holds for the stated flows; accumulation in the loop lies outside the example.

prose:
The goal of this worked example is a vapour pressure from the Antoine equation, and the outcome is a calculated pressure for acetone at a stated temperature, checked against a measured value. You need the Antoine constants for the compound and the temperature. The Antoine equation gives the common logarithm (the logarithm in the Antoine equation) of P (vapour pressure, in bar) as A minus the quotient B divided by the sum of T (temperature, in degrees Celsius) and C, where A, B, C are empirical constants fitted to measured vapour pressure data. The constants are bound to their units, and a constant set fitted for pressure in bar returns a wrong pressure in any other unit: check the unit of the constant set before any arithmetic.

The Antoine constants for acetone are A = 4.42, B = 1312, and C = 240, with pressure in bar and temperature in degrees Celsius. At a temperature of 40 degrees Celsius, the denominator T + C is 280. The quotient B divided by 280 is 4.686, and 4.42 minus 4.686 gives a logarithm of -0.266. The vapour pressure is 0.54 bar. Each step carries one operation, and the denominator is the step where sign and bracket errors enter: C is added to the temperature before the division, never after.

The check compares the calculated pressure with a measurement at the same temperature. A measured value for the same temperature is 0.55 bar, and the difference from the calculated value is 0.01 bar. The difference sits at the level of the scatter in the data behind the constant fit, and the calculated value stands as the estimate to carry forward. The constants hold over the fitted temperature range of the source data; extrapolation beyond that range lies outside the example, and a temperature outside the range needs a constant set fitted there. Keep the temperature, the constants, and the pressure in one unit system from the first line of the working to the last, and record the constant source beside the result for a repeat calculation from the record alone.

You need the particle diameter, both densities, and the fluid viscosity. The Stokes relation (the drag balance for a sphere in creeping flow, giving terminal velocity from particle and fluid properties) returns v (terminal velocity, in metres per second) from d (particle diameter) and the fluid properties, and the relation carries a condition: the flow around the particle must be creeping flow, and the check at the end tests that condition.

Particle diameter is 80 micrometres. Particle density is 2650 kg per cubic metre, and fluid density is 1000 kg per cubic metre. The density difference is 1650 kg per cubic metre. Fluid viscosity is 0.001 pascal seconds, and gravitational acceleration is 9.81 metres per second squared. Terminal velocity is 0.0058 metres per second. The check tests the condition the relation carries. The particle Reynolds number is 0.46, inside the creeping-flow range of the Stokes relation. The velocity stands, and the check is part of the result rather than an extra: a Reynolds number outside the creeping-flow range would void the drag balance behind the velocity, and a drag relation for the transitional range would replace the Stokes relation. points: Specific capacitance of the carbon electrode was 248 farads per gram at a current density of 1 ampere per gram.
Capacitance retention at a current density of 20 amperes per gram was 86 %.
Energy density of the assembled cell was 31 watt hours per kilogram.

definitions: supercapacitor = an electrochemical cell that stores charge in the double layer at an electrode surface
specific capacitance = capacitance divided by the mass of active material in one electrode, in farads per gram
energy density = stored energy divided by the mass of the assembled cell, in watt hours per kilogram
prose: Supercapacitors (electrochemical cells that store charge in the double layer at an electrode surface) store far less energy than batteries, and the gap sits in the electrode material. A porous carbon electrode was prepared from a biomass precursor by carbonisation and chemical activation, with the activation conditions set to match the pore width to the electrolyte ion size. Electrodes were tested in a symmetric cell, and capacitance was measured by galvanostatic discharge. Specific capacitance (capacitance divided by the mass of active material in one electrode, in farads per gram) of the carbon electrode was 248 farads per gram at a current density of 1 ampere per gram. Capacitance retention at a current density of 20 amperes per gram was 86 %. Energy density (stored energy divided by the mass of the assembled cell, in watt hours per kilogram) of the assembled cell was 31 watt hours per kilogram. Capacitance retention after 10000 charge and discharge cycles was 94 %. Retention at the higher current density assigns the rate performance to the matched pore width rather than to the total surface area, and the cycle retention shows the pore structure surviving repeated charge movement. A biomass-derived carbon with pores matched to the electrolyte gives a supercapacitor electrode with high capacitance at high rate from a low-cost precursor.

prose: Mineral carbonation (the reaction of carbon dioxide with a silicate mineral to form a solid carbonate) converts carbon dioxide into a solid carbonate, and the route is limited by the rate at which silicate rock reacts. Carbon dioxide mineralization was studied on olivine (a magnesium silicate mineral) in a stirred reactor with a bicarbonate-bearing solution. The study tested whether fine grinding and the bicarbonate solution together raise the reaction extent to a level a process could use. Carbon dioxide uptake was 0.42 tonnes per tonne of olivine. Reaction extent (the fraction of the olivine converted to carbonate) reached 78 % in 6 hours. The reactor operated at 185 degrees Celsius and 40 bar. Carbonate purity in the solid product was 96 %. Energy demand was 1.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide converted. The extent at the stated time assigns the rate gain to the solution chemistry rather than to grinding alone: ground olivine in water alone reacts more slowly under the same conditions. A mineralization route on olivine at the measured extent carries a carbonate product that holds the carbon in solid form, with the energy demand of grinding and reactor heating as the cost the process must recover.

points: Unprotected steel corrodes at 0.12 mm per year in the splash zone.
Coating systems on the foundations carry a design life of 15 years.
The foundations are monopiles of 8 metres diameter in water 30 metres deep.

definitions: monopile = a single large-diameter steel tube driven into the seabed as a foundation
mudline = the level of the seabed surface around the foundation
cathodic protection = protection of steel by making the steel the cathode of an electrochemical cell, with a sacrificial or driven anode

prose:
Offshore wind turbines stand on steel foundations in seawater, and corrosion of the foundations sets a large part of the inspection and maintenance burden across a wind farm. Unprotected steel corrodes at 0.12 mm per year in the splash zone (the band of the foundation alternately wetted by waves and exposed to air). Coating systems on the foundations carry a design life of 15 years. Cathodic protection (protection of steel by making the steel the cathode of an electrochemical cell, with a sacrificial or driven anode) covers the submerged steel, and the splash zone and the mudline (the level of the seabed surface around the foundation) sit outside the protected length. The foundations are monopiles (single large-diameter steel tubes driven into the seabed as a foundation) of 8 metres diameter in water 30 metres deep. The turbine design life is 25 years, and the coating design life ends well inside the turbine design life.

Corrosion behaviour in the splash zone is established from coupon programmes and from inspection records on older structures. The mudline is a different case. Biofouling covers the steel at the mudline, sediment moves across the surface, and the corrosion rate of foundation steel under combined biofouling and sediment cover is a missing piece of knowledge: published rates come from clean steel or from buried steel, and neither condition matches the mudline.

The study measures corrosion at the mudline of operating foundations. Coupons and electrical resistance probes are mounted at the mudline and at reference depths on the same foundations, and retrieval across the exposure period gives a rate under the fouling and sediment conditions the foundations actually carry.

points: Reported areal productivity spans 12 to 25 g per square metre per day across published pond studies.
The pilot pond has an area of 0.5 hectares.
Pond operating depth is 0.3 metres.
Harvest concentration in the pilot pond reaches 0.8 g per litre.
definitions: areal productivity = biomass produced per unit pond area per day, in grams per square metre per day
flocculation = the clumping of suspended cells into aggregates that settle
prose:
Algal biofuel production grows algae in open ponds and converts the harvested biomass to fuel, and the economics of the route turn on the productivity a pond sustains outdoors. Reported areal productivity (biomass produced per unit pond area per day, in grams per square metre per day) spans 12 to 25 g per square metre per day across published pond studies. The spread across studies is wide, and the studies differ in climate, pond depth, mixing, and harvest practice. The pilot pond has an area of 0.5 hectares. Pond operating depth is 0.3 metres. Harvest concentration in the pilot pond reaches 0.8 g per litre.

Established pond operation controls temperature by depth, controls acidity by carbon dioxide addition, and harvests by flocculation (the clumping of suspended cells into aggregates that settle) and settling. The controlled variables are the cheap ones. Productivity under variable light is the uncontrolled case: light at the pond surface changes with cloud cover on a timescale of minutes, algae in the mixed pond move between surface light and depth shade, and the productivity response to that fluctuating light field is a missing piece of knowledge. Steady-light laboratory measurements give a photosynthesis response that the pond never sees, and pond models built on the steady response mispredict the outdoor record in both directions.

The study measures the productivity response of the pond culture to fluctuating light. The pilot pond carries continuous light logging at the surface and at depth, and a laboratory rig exposes the same culture to light programmes replayed from the pond record, with productivity measured on both routes across the same periods.

points: The scan ran from 10 to 80 degrees.
Step size was 0.02 degrees, with a counting time of 2 seconds per step.

Phase fractions from the refinement carry an estimated uncertainty of 1.5 % by mass.
definitions: Rietveld refinement = a least-squares fit of a calculated diffraction pattern to the measured pattern, returning phase fractions
internal standard = a phase of known amount added to the sample, against which the amorphous content is measured
phase fraction = the mass fraction of one crystalline phase in the sample
limits: The method quantifies crystalline phases in the stated scan range; amorphous content enters through the internal standard, and a phase below the detection level of the refinement carries no reported fraction.
prose:
Phase quantification by X-ray diffraction used a powder diffractometer with a copper anode tube and a position-sensitive detector. Samples were ground to a fine powder, mixed with the internal standard, and back-loaded into the sample holder to limit preferred orientation of the crystallites. The scan ran from 10 to 80 degrees. Step size was 0.02 degrees, with a counting time of 2 seconds per step. Tube voltage was 40 kilovolts, and tube current was 30 milliamperes. The sample carried 10 % by mass of corundum as an internal standard (a phase of known amount added to the sample, against which the amorphous content is measured). The holder rotated during the scan, and the rotation averaged the crystallite orientations presented to the beam. A repeat scan of the same preparation checked the stability of the pattern before the refinement began.

Phase fractions (the mass fraction of one crystalline phase in the sample) were obtained by Rietveld refinement (a least-squares fit of a calculated diffraction pattern to the measured pattern, returning phase fractions). The refinement fitted the scale factor of each crystalline phase, the lattice parameters of each phase, a background function, and a peak-shape function, in that order, with the instrument profile fixed from a standard scan. The internal standard anchors the amorphous content: the refinement returns crystalline fractions normalised to the crystalline total, and the known standard addition rescales the fractions to the whole sample, with the remainder reported as amorphous content. Phase fractions from the refinement carry an estimated uncertainty of 1.5 % by mass, estimated from repeat preparations of a reference mixture. The method quantifies crystalline phases in the stated scan range; amorphous content enters through the internal standard, and a phase below the detection level of the refinement carries no reported fraction.

prose:
Dissolved oxygen was measured with an optical probe (a probe in which oxygen quenches the luminescence of a sensing dye, and the quenching gives the oxygen concentration). Calibration used two points, a zero point and a span point, in that order. Zero calibration used a sodium sulfite solution at 20 g per litre, with the probe held in the solution until the reading was stable at zero. The span point used air-saturated water, prepared by bubbling air through water at constant temperature until successive readings agreed. Air-saturated water at 25 degrees Celsius gave the span value (the reading assigned to air-saturated water at the calibration temperature) of 8.3 mg per litre. Barometric pressure at calibration was 101 kilopascals, and the probe applied the pressure correction internally from a manual entry.

Temperature compensation used the temperature sensor in the probe cap, and the calibration record carries the temperature of both calibration solutions. Readings were taken with the probe moving slowly through the sample, and a reading taken in still water was discarded. Acceptance allows a drift of 0.2 mg per litre over 24 hours, tested by returning the probe to air-saturated water at the end of the field day. Calibration was confirmed by Winkler titration (a chemical titration that fixes the oxygen in the sample and titrates the released iodine) on a split sample, and the probe and titration values agreed within the acceptance drift. The calibration record for each probe carries the date, the operator, the solution batch, and the two calibration readings, and the record travels with the probe data file. Probes failing the drift test were recalibrated, and a second failure removed the sensing cap from service. Calibration holds for the stated temperature and pressure route, and a probe used outside the drift acceptance carries no valid calibration.

Electricity drawn was 250 kilowatts, and the coefficient of performance was 3.4.
The source temperature was 35 degrees Celsius, and the delivery temperature was 72 degrees Celsius.
Operation was metered over 11 months.
Avoided gas use corresponds to 1280 tonnes of carbon dioxide per year.
Payback on the installed cost was 4.6 years at the metered performance.

limits: A higher delivery temperature lowers the coefficient of performance; a colder source during a production shutdown lies outside the metered record.
Long-term degradation of the compressor lies beyond the metered period.
prose:
The retrofit replaced a gas boiler with an industrial heat pump lifting waste heat from the process cooling circuit to the site heating circuit. Heat delivered by the retrofit heat pump was 850 kilowatts. Electricity drawn was 250 kilowatts, and the coefficient of performance (the ratio of heat delivered to electricity drawn) was 3.4. The source temperature was 35 degrees Celsius, and the delivery temperature was 72 degrees Celsius. Operation was metered over 11 months. Avoided gas use corresponds to 1280 tonnes of carbon dioxide per year. Payback on the installed cost was 4.6 years at the metered performance.

The principal result is the coefficient of performance at the tested lift (the temperature difference between the delivery temperature and the source temperature): the heat pump delivered the site heat load at the stated source and delivery temperatures across the metered period, through the seasonal swing of both circuits. Performance at part load was weaker than performance near full load, and the metered average carries the part-load hours of the shoulder seasons. Two scope conditions bound the claim. The delivery temperature was held at the stated value by the heating circuit control, and a higher delivery temperature lowers the coefficient of performance by raising the lift. The source was process waste heat at the stated temperature, and a colder source in a production shutdown lies outside the metered record. Refrigerant leakage across the period was below the detection of the charge record, and long-term degradation of the compressor lies beyond the metered period. Within the tested scope, the retrofit stands as a measured replacement for the boiler duty the heat pump took over, at the metered coefficient of performance.

prose: Rheogram (a plot of viscosity against shear rate) of a xanthan gum solution on a rotational rheometer, cone-and-plate geometry. The rheogram covers shear rates from 0.1 to 500 per second. Measurement temperature was 25 degrees Celsius. Curves are means of 3 replicate samples; error bars are one standard deviation of the mean. The fitted power-law index (the exponent in the relation of viscosity to shear rate) was 0.42, and viscosity fell across the whole range: the solution is shear-thinning (viscosity falling as shear rate rises) at every measured rate, with no low-shear plateau.

definitions: E = cell potential, in volts
E° = standard cell potential, the cell potential at the standard composition, in volts
R = gas constant
T = absolute temperature, in kelvin

prose:
Cell potential changes with the composition of the cell, and the Nernst equation carries that change in a single relation. The cell potential E (the voltage of an electrochemical cell under a stated composition, in volts) is the central quantity. The Nernst equation gives E as the standard cell potential E° minus the product of R, T, and the natural logarithm of Q, divided by the product of n and F. In the equation, E° is the standard cell potential (the cell potential at the standard composition), R is the gas constant, T is the absolute temperature, Q is the reaction quotient (the ratio of product activities to reactant activities), n is the number of electrons transferred in the cell reaction, and F is the Faraday constant (the charge of one mole of electrons). At the boundary case of Q of 1, the logarithm is 0 and E equals the standard cell potential.

R is 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin, and F is 96485 coulombs per mole. The standard cell potential E° is 1.10 V for the zinc and copper cell. At a temperature T of 298 kelvin, R times T divided by F is 0.0257 V. The electron number n for the zinc and copper reaction is 2. At a reaction quotient Q of 0.05, the natural logarithm of Q is -3.00. The correction term is 0.0386 V. The cell potential E at that quotient is 1.14 V. The potential stands above the standard potential because the quotient sits below the boundary value: products are scarcer than the standard composition, and the cell reaction has further to run before the quotient reaches the equilibrium value. The equation holds for a cell reaction with the electrodes at equilibrium, at the stated temperature, and activity coefficients are carried inside the activities in Q.
